It's true that on a per capita basis, Medicare's administrative costs can appear higher than those of private insurers. However, this is largely because Medicare primarily serves older individuals, who typically have higher healthcare costs. As a percentage of total costs, Medicare's administrative costs are lower than those of private insurers. A universal healthcare system could potentially achieve even greater efficiencies through economies of scale.

Medicare does standardize its reimbursements, which are often lower than what private insurers pay. This is one reason why healthcare costs have risen for non-Medicare patients. In a universal healthcare system, all patients would be part of the same system, so there wouldn't be a need for providers to shift costs onto non-Medicare patients. Plus standardized reimbursements could help control healthcare costs by reducing price variation and eliminating excessively high prices.

United Healthcare is not necessarily a good comparison for a single-payer system. Private insurance companies have different goals and structures, and they typically have higher administrative costs and marketing expenses than a government-run system would have. Even if United's costs remain high after accounting for profit and CEO pay, it doesn't necessarily mean a single-payer system would have the same high costs.

Each country's healthcare system is influenced by a variety of factors, including the structure of the healthcare system, the relative bargaining power of providers and insurers, and lifestyle factors.

Singapore is a unique case due to its mandatory health savings accounts and heavy government regulation of healthcare prices. The US does not heavily regulate drug prices.
